item.title: Taiwan warns Canada faces the China risks Carney has cautioned against
item.description:
Taiwan warns Canada faces the China risks Carney has cautioned against
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has tried to deepen trade ties with China.ByROB GILLIES Associated PressNovember 21, 2026, 12:39 PM
HALIFAX, Nova Scotia -- Taiwan’s deputy foreign minister warned on Saturday that Prime Minister Mark Carney risks exposing Canada to the very economic coercion he has cautioned against by deepening trade ties with China, saying that Taiwan has learned the hard way that dependence on Beijing comes with consequences.
“We worry. We worry,” Chen Ming-chi told The Associated Press in an interview at the Halifax International Security Forum when asked about Carney’s efforts to improve relations with China.
Carney has warned that major powers are using economic integration as a weapon, citing U.S. tariffs and China’s restrictions on critical minerals. He has urged middle powers to diversify their trade relationships to avoid economic coercion.
Chen praised Carney’s speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, but questioned whether Canada should deepen ties with countries that don’t share its democratic values.
“Who do you want to choose as your partners?” he asked.
“You have your own history. You have two Michaels,” Chen said, referring to former Canadian diplomat Michael Kovrig and businessman Michael Spavor, whose ne arly three-year detention in China prompted accusations of hostage diplomacy.
The two were arrested in 2018 shortly after Canada detained Huawei executive Meng Wanzhou on a U.S. extradition request. They were released in September 2021, the same day Meng returned to China. Beijing denied their detention was politically motivated.
Chen’s warning came days after Carney met with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen and agreed to additional tariff reductions as Canada seeks to diversify trade during U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war.

item.title: Mexico detains top cartel boss 'El Chapo Isidro,' setting off a burst of violence in Sinaloa
item.description:
Mexico detains top cartel boss 'El Chapo Isidro,' setting off a burst of violence in Sinaloa
Mexican authorities have captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores who is known as “El Chapo Isidro.”ByMEGAN JANETSKY Associated Press, FABIOLA SÁNCHEZ Associated Press, and MARTÍN URISTA Associated PressNovember 21, 2026, 8:23 AM
GUASAVE, Mexico -- Gunfire rang out, trucks burned and Mexican forces clashed with cartel gunmen in the state of Sinaloa overnight as Mexican authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro.”
Meza Flores was one of the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives. He climbed the cartel ranks to lead the Beltrán Leyva cartel and later became the leader of his own group, the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. The United States had a $5 million reward offer for information leading to his arrest, and he was wanted for trafficking drugs to the U.S. and illegally carrying firearms.
Mexico's government said in a report early Saturday that intelligence from the Trump administration helped authorities capture him, but provided few details about how authorities in Mexico and the United States coordinated to detain Meza Flores.
He was also a key ally to “Los Mayos,” a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, which was designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the Trump administration last year. His capture represents a blow to the cartel as it fights with another faction for control of the northern Mexican state.
Authorities in the United States and Mexico celebrated the arrest as a security win. U.S. President Donald Trump has pressured Mexico's government to go after criminal groups.
As a fierce firefight settled into a tense calm Saturday, experts warn that picking off capos could set off another wave of violence in a region already caught up in a power struggle between warring cartel factions.

item.title: Black music producer's lawyer hails landmark ruling as French court finds racist police violence
item.description:
Black music producer's lawyer hails landmark ruling as French court finds racist police violence
A French court has acknowledged the racist nature of a violent incident involving police officers and sentenced them to prisonBySAMUEL PETREQUIN Associated PressNovember 21, 2026, 6:37 AM
Share
PARIS -- The lawyer for a Black man who was beaten up by three French police officers hailed a “historic ruling” on Saturday after a court acknowledged the racist nature of the violence and sentenced them to between one and two years in prison.
The assault on Michel Zecler, a music producer, took place six years ago during the coronavirus pandemic and was caught on camera. It showed the officers repeatedly punching him, using a truncheon and tear gas against him for no apparent reason.
Zecler told The Associated Press after the incident that the officers hurled repeated insults at him, including a very strong racist epithet.
“What is very important is that the racist nature of the violence he suffered has been recognized," Zecler's lawyer, Serge Money, told France Info. “As a legal professional, one can only be satisfied. This is a first.”
Money said that from the very beginning of the proceedings, Zecler maintained that he had been racially insulted, whereas the defendants’ accounts were somewhat inconsistent.
"Ultimately, they were convicted of lying, as the falsification of written records was established,” he said. The verdict was issued late Friday in Paris.
Videos published showed the violent arrest of Zecler in the 17th arrondissement of the French capital. The three officers intended to stop him for not wearing a face mask during the restrictions imposed because of the pandemic.
The video images, obtained by the AP, both from a security camera inside the studio and filmed by neighbors outside, showed officers following Zecler inside his music studio, where they could be seen repeatedly punching him and beating him with a truncheon.

item.title: Missile attack on Zelenskyy's hometown in central Ukraine kills 2 and wounds scores
item.description:
Missile attack on Zelenskyy's hometown in central Ukraine kills 2 and wounds scores
A Russian strike on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown, Kryvyi Rih, has killed two people and wounded 60 othersBySAMYA KULLAB Associated Press and ELISE MORTON Associated PressNovember 21, 2026, 5:55 AM
KYIV, Ukraine -- A Russian strike on the center of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s hometown, Kryvyi Rih, killed two people and wounded 60 others, local officials said Saturday.
A 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman were killed in the attack Friday night on the city in central Ukraine, Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of the city administration, wrote on Telegram. Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the regional military administration, said 60 people were wounded, including six children.
The strike caused four fires and damaged about 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools and an industrial facility, as well as businesses and vehicles, Vilkul said.
The attack fits the pattern of Moscow’s heavy responses to eye-catching Ukrainian attacks, such as the ones this week on the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to illegally annexed Crimea.
The missile attack came hours after two Russian missiles and a suspected drone came down in Poland, in what its prime minister said was likely a provocation timed to coincide with European military exercises in his country for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine.
European troops were taking part Friday in an unprecedented two-week military exercise that began Nov. 9 in southeastern Poland. Forces are preparing for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine aimed at helping to stabilize the country and rebuild its military. European countries previously have expressed alarm at what they deem to be Russia’s attempts to destabilize the continent.

item.title: Athlete swims in Strait of Hormuz to highlight Iran war's impact on wildlife
item.description:
Athlete swims in Strait of Hormuz to highlight Iran war's impact on wildlife
British endurance swimmer Lewis Pugh has swum the Strait of Hormuz to highlight environmental threats during ongoing conflictByKWIYEON HA Associated Press and SYLVIA HUI Associated PressNovember 21, 2026, 12:06 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
LONDON -- British endurance swimmer Lewis Pugh has swum in the North Pole and Antarctica to draw attention to environmental causes. But battling freezing waters and extreme conditions hasn't prepared him for his latest challenge: swimming the Strait of Hormuz while tankers are attacked and blown up nearby.
Pugh, who is a United Nations Patron of the Oceans, spent three days this week swimming parts of the dangerous waterway to highlight how the war with Iran threatens the area's habitat and wildlife.
Wearing only swimming trunks, goggles and a cap bearing the U.N. logo, the athlete started from the Musandam peninsula, on the southern tip of the strait, and ended by rounding the Cape of Hormuz, completing about 15 kilometers (9.3 miles) in total. Pugh is believed to be the first person to undertake a long-distance swim there since the war started.
The swimmer said that minutes after he entered the water on Monday, he heard two loud explosions that rocked the sea.
“I looked up and I could see that an oil tanker about four kilometers away had been hit,” he told The Associated Press after he returned to London. “The explosion was so loud, two booms, and then fighter jets coming in. And at that moment I realized we have to get out of here right now.”
Pugh, 56, managed to finish his feat after more stops and starts, including passing another vessel that sent fireballs into the sky after it was attacked.
“Most people, when they think about the Strait of Hormuz, they think of a shipping lane,” he said. “But it is also one of the most beautiful places I have ever been … it's one of the treasure troves of the natural world.”

item.title: Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, former South Africa deputy president and UN Women chief, dies at 71
item.description:
Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, former South Africa deputy president and UN Women chief, dies at 71
Former South African Deputy President Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka has died at 71ByMOGOMOTSI MAGOME Associated PressNovember 20, 2026, 9:36 PM
Share
JOHANNESBURG -- JOHANNESBURG (AP) — Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, South Africa's first female deputy president and a United Nations under-secretary-general, has died at age 71, the South African government announced Friday.
Mlambo-Ngcuka, a former anti-apartheid activist and lawmaker in the South African Parliament, was deputy president from 2005 until 2008. She also served as minister of minerals and energy and deputy minister of trade and industry. She served as under-secretary-general and executive director of U.N. Women from 2013 to 2021.
The exact date and location of her death were not immediately shared by the government or her political party, the African National Congress.
Mlambo-Ngcuka was part of South Africa's first democratic Parliament for the ANC after the end of apartheid and white minority rule in 1994 when Nelson Mandela was elected the country's first democratically elected leader.
Tributes following her death lauded her contribution to South Africa's struggle for liberation and new democracy and the role she played at the U.N., where she championed women's rights and gender equality.
“Mama Phumzile was a distinguished leader of our movement and a dedicated servant of the people. She made history as the first woman to serve as Deputy President of South Africa,” the ANC said in a statement Friday.
U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres expressed condolences and called her “a lifelong champion of the rights and empowerment of women and girls.”

item.title: All 146 Air Niugini plane passengers and crew safe after an emergency landing in Philippines
item.description:
All 146 Air Niugini plane passengers and crew safe after an emergency landing in Philippines
An Air Niugini plane carrying 146 passengers and crew from Hong Kong to Papua New Guinea has safely made an emergency landing in a southern Philippine city due to a warning of a possible engine fireByThe Associated PressNovember 20, 2026, 9:15 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
MANILA, Philippines -- An Air Niugini plane carrying 146 passengers and crew from Hong Kong to Papua New Guinea safely made an emergency landing Saturday in a southern Philippine city due to an indication of a possible engine fire, Philippine aviation officials said.
There were no reports of injuries among the 137 passengers and nine crewmembers, who disembarked through emergency slides of the Boeing 767-383ER after it diverted from its route and landed at the Davao International Airport, the Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines said.
The pilots reported that they detected, through an indicator, possible sparks or fire in the right engine. They undertook safety procedures and requested to make an unscheduled landing in Davao shortly after midnight, Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines spokesperson Eric Apolonio said without elaborating, adding that an investigation will include the accounts of the pilots.

item.title: Magnitude 6.7 earthquake shakes Peru's Andes
item.description:
Magnitude 6.7 earthquake shakes Peru's Andes
A magnitude 6.7 earthquake has shaken the Andes in central Peru with no immediate reports of damage or casualtiesByThe Associated PressNovember 20, 2026, 7:40 PM
Share
LIMA, Peru -- A magnitude 6.7 earthquake shook the Andes in central Peru on Friday with no immediate reports of damage or casualties.
The U.S. Geological Survey said the earthquake struck at 7:09 p.m. local time. Its epicenter was in the Andes, 34 kilometers (21 miles) north of Junín, at a depth of 108 kilometers (67 miles).
Peru’s Geophysical Institute said no damages or casualties had been reported. And the mayor of Carhuamayo near the epicenter, Abdel Vega, also told a local television station that there were no reports of victims or material damages.
The earthquake was felt in the Peruvian capital, prompting residents to rush into the streets.

Peru lies along the “Ring of Fire,” a 40,000-kilometer (25,000-mile) arc of volcanoes and fault lines around the Pacific Basin, where most of the world’s earthquakes occur.
In August, a 6.7 magnitude earthquake in the Peruvian Andes left two people injured and damaged several homes, health centers and schools, while in July, a 5.5-magnitude quake in the Junín region resulted in six deaths and 30 injuries.

item.title: Bolivian festival seeks to return guinea pig to nations' rituals
item.description:
Bolivian festival seeks to return guinea pig to nations' rituals
Guinea pigs, known as cuy in the Andes region, have enjoyed a day in their honor in Bolivia with races, and beauty and weight contests, organized by students promoting the rodent’s nutritional and economic value to Bolivian householdsByCARLOS VALDEZ Associated PressNovember 20, 2026, 5:58 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
EL ALTO, Bolivia -- Guinea pigs, known as cuy in the Andes region, enjoyed a day in their honor Friday in Bolivia with races and beauty and weight contests organized by students promoting the rodent’s nutritional and economic value to Bolivian households.
Domesticated thousands of years ago in the Bolivian Andes, the cuy was considered sacred by ancient cultures and was used in ceremonies and as a food source. But raising them has nearly disappeared in recent decades as other meats have gained favor.
Students in the animal science and livestock program at the Public University of El Alto, a city neighboring La Paz, organized a race to reward the fastest cuy, a weigh-in to identify the heaviest and a runway show to crown the most stylish. The event brought together students and local farmers in the city, which sits at an elevation of 3,800 meters (12,500 feet).
“Our ancestors raised guinea pigs for centuries for food and rituals in the Andes,” said César Quispe, an instructor in the animal science program. “Their meat has high nutritional value and a low fat content.”
A cuy weighing 2.5 kilograms (5.5 pounds) from El Alto’s Kallutaca farm took the prize for the heaviest, while another from a different farm finished first in the speed race.
A food court offered a wide variety of traditional dishes, including roasted and baked cuys, cuys on skewers, and burgers and sausages made from the rodent’s meat.
Quispe said the decline of the cuy began during the colonial era, and today per capita consumption in Bolivia is low.

item.title: Haiti strikes deal with El Salvador to build new prisons after minister visit
item.description:
Haiti strikes deal with El Salvador to build new prisons after minister visit
Haiti announces an agreement with El Salvador for the construction of a new prisonByEVENS SANON Associated Press, YOLANDA MAGAÑA Associated Press, and AND ANNA-CATHERINE BRIGIDA Associated PressNovember 20, 2026, 5:49 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
PORT-AU-PRINCE, Haiti -- Haiti announced an agreement with El Salvador Friday for the construction of new prisons as the two countries increase cooperation following the Central American country's deployment of troops to fight gangs in Haiti.
This announcement by Haitian Minister of Justice and Public Security Patrick Pélissier follows his official mission to El Salvador. The first prison will be launched soon with the prime minister ordering it to be expedited. It will be one of three prisons built by a Salvadoran company in collaboration with a Haitian firm, the minister said.
Gangs control an estimated 70% of Haiti’s capital and swaths of land in the country’s central region.
Pélissier praised the notorious Salvadoran maximum security prison CECOT, which he visited while in the Central American country for an international conference. El Salvador has been under a state of exception since 2022 that has imprisoned more than 90,000 people with no access to family visits. The U.S. has also deported Venezuelans and Salvadorans to the CECOT and they have denounced torture there after release.
“Once you enter, there is no hope of ever seeing the outside world again,” Pélissier said.
Haiti has struggled to find proper infrastructure to hold those arrested after powerful gangs raided the country’s two biggest prisons in 2024 and released thousands of inmates. Haiti's prisons have long been notorious for severe overcrowding, with human rights experts warning that prisoners sleep standing and hundreds have died in recent years.
